The Perfect tenses can be used to talk about how something in the past relates to the present.
You can use the Perfect Infinitive after certain link verbs (appear, seem) to talk about a time period in the past.

For example:
He seems to have already been hired.
They appear to have finished the presentation.

The structure of the Perfect Infinitive is:
subject + appear/seem + to have + past participle
She seems to have taken her meeting with the director seriously.
He seems to have not explained the task very well.
There appears to have been some miscommunication during the hiring process.

Instructions: Complete the following steps. Fill in the Self Assessment.

images.text:
Denise: Good morning, Adam. I'm sorry to have kept you waiting.
Adam: Good morning, Ms. Moore. How are you?
Denise: I'm good, thanks. The quarterly report shows our numbers are finally starting to climb for selling workbooks in the school market. It appears our pitch and marketing plan have been successful. What can I do for you?
Adam: Ms. Moore, there appears to have been some miscommunication during the hiring process. It seems as though the responsibilities the company has given me are not a good match for my personality.
Denise: Go on.

Adam: It seems I have come to the realization that I am a more holistic thinker. I love creative writing because it transports me to another place. I also love the research and conversations that are required in order to come up with great stories. As an editorial assistant, I'm looking for missing commas all day long.
Denise: It looks like you haven't been told everything you need to have been told about publishing, Adam. I would say your tasks have not been well explained. It also sounds as though we have had similar experiences. I, too, felt that I wasn't well suited for editing work when I first started. The reality is that you need to have both skill sets. You need to be a visionary so as to be able to undertake large projects. You also need to be attentive to detail so as to catch small mistakes and inconsistencies.

Adam: What do you suggest?
Denise: You will start enjoying detailed work more as you get better at it. Then, as circumstances change, you will be exposed to a greater variety of tasks. You will do some creative writing and sit in on brainstorming sessions. Those will be fascinating conversations. Listen, to expedite things, why don't we transfer you to my team? I can be a sort of mentor for helping you to adjust.
Adam: Wow, Ms. Moore! Thank you!
Denise: You're welcome, Adam. It seems we have really understood each other.
